name: French White
lede: French White is a pale, greyish pink-lilac in the 1930 Maerz and Paul dictionary, and also an older name from the paint trade for a fine lead white.

sections.title: Two things with one name
sections.body:
The color French White comes from Maerz and Paul's *Dictionary of Color* of 1930, which lists it on plate 42 and gives 1845 as the first recorded use [1]. The swatch is a greyish pink-lilac, not a white at all; the nearest named colors are [[thistle]] and Dull Lavender [1][2].

A second French white existed long before the dictionary, in the artists' colorman's trade [3]. There it was a lead white, and the books list it among the many names for the same pigment [3].

sections.title: The pigment: a lead white
sections.body:
The Pigment Compendium records that Field (1835) counted French white as a fine lead white, a name for the same thing as blanc d'argent and silver white [3]. Scott Taylor (1885) adds that it was also a synonym for ceruse, the old name for white lead [3]. Salter (1869) describes it as brought from Paris in the form of drops, very white, but with less body than flake white [3].

Books disagree about how pure it was. Church (1901) doubted that the French blanc d'argent was a pure, hydrate-free lead carbonate and judged most of it to be ordinary good-quality flake white [4]. The compendium itself warns that "silver white" could have other meanings, so the old names need care [4]. Its lead white entry also lists French white among many synonyms, alongside Dutch, Roman, Venetian and Hamburg white [5].

It was a workaday ingredient as well as a fine one: a recipe from Fishwick (1795-1816) for common red paint mixes Bristol red and Venetian red with French white [6].

sections.title: Why the swatch is not white
sections.body: No source here links the pigment to the dictionary swatch. The dictionary file is a fashion and textile list, and its date, 1845, is a first record of the name in that field, not of the paint [1]. The two meanings share a word and little else; treat the screen swatch as one dictionary's idea of a faintly tinted off-white, near [[lilac]] in hue and approximate on any screen [1][2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: The swatch measures about 73 in lightness and sits in the neutrals family [2]. Its nearest archive color is Thistle, 7.8 units away on the color-difference scale, which is a loose match rather than a twin [2]. No book discusses this swatch as a painted color, so we draw no conclusions from the archive for it [2].
